course.title: Product Management
course.description: How software products actually get built and shipped - discovering real customer problems, deciding what to build next, and turning a fuzzy idea into a spec, a launch, and a measurable outcome. Structure adapted from open product-management curricula on OER Commons (CC BY 4.0); all explanations original.

questions.prompt: The core job of a product manager is best described as...
options: writing most of the production code
deciding what to build and why, then aligning others to ship it
managing the engineers as their direct boss
questions.explanation: A PM sets direction and builds shared understanding of what to build and why - see 'What a product manager does (and doesn't).'

questions.prompt: A 'job to be done' framing focuses on...
options: the feature the customer requested by name
the progress a customer is trying to make in their life
the price the customer will pay
questions.explanation: Jobs-to-be-done looks at the underlying progress the customer wants, not the surface request - see 'Discovering customer problems.'

questions.prompt: In the RICE scoring model, the four factors are Reach, Impact, Confidence, and...
questions.explanation: RICE = (Reach x Impact x Confidence) / Effort. Effort is the denominator.

questions.prompt: A user story is usually written in the form 'As a ___, I want ___, so that ___.' The final clause captures the...
options: reason or benefit the user is after
questions.explanation: The 'so that' clause states the benefit, keeping the story tied to real value.

questions.prompt: A North Star metric is meant to...
options: capture the core value customers get, guiding the whole team
count how many meetings the team holds
questions.explanation: A North Star metric expresses delivered customer value and aligns everyone - see 'Defining and tracking metrics.'

questions.prompt: In an A/B test, the purpose of the control group is to...
options: receive the new experience being tested
provide a baseline of the current experience for comparison
reduce the number of users in the test
questions.explanation: The control keeps the existing experience so you can measure the change against a baseline.

questions.prompt: A product roadmap is most useful when it communicates...
options: exact ship dates for every feature a year out
outcomes and priorities over time, with more certainty near-term
a fixed contract that can never change
the personal preferences of the loudest stakeholder
questions.explanation: Good roadmaps express intent and priority, staying flexible further out - see 'Roadmapping and stakeholder alignment.'

questions.prompt: Go-to-market planning primarily answers...
options: how the right customers will find, understand, and adopt the product
who reports to whom on the org chart
questions.explanation: Go-to-market is about reaching and activating the target customer - see 'Go-to-market and launch.'

lessons.title: What a product manager does (and doesn't)
lessons.grammar_note: A PM owns the 'why' and 'what'; design owns much of the 'how it feels' and engineering owns the 'how it is built.' Authority here comes from clarity and trust, not from a reporting line.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what a product manager is responsible for, name what the role is not, and describe how a PM creates influence without direct authority. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, in one phrase, what is the core job of a PM?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A product manager is responsible for deciding what to build, why it matters, and in what order, and then for getting a team of specialists to agree and ship it. The PM sits at the intersection of the customer's needs, the business's goals, and what is technically feasible, and keeps those three in balance. Crucially, a PM usually has no direct reports on the team: engineers, designers, and analysts do not answer to the PM on an org chart. Influence therefore comes from doing the homework - knowing the customer and the data better than anyone, writing clearly, and building trust - not from giving orders. A common shorthand is that the PM owns the problem and the priorities, while the team owns the solution.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A PM who does the job well: notices that new users abandon signup, interviews ten of them, discovers a confusing verification step, frames the problem crisply, and works with design and engineering to test a fix. A PM overstepping: dictating the exact button color and database schema while ignoring why users churn. That is doing the specialists' jobs and skipping the PM's own. Another anti-pattern: acting as a 'feature order-taker,' passing along whatever the loudest executive requests without asking what problem it solves. The strong move in each case is to return to the customer problem and the evidence, then let the experts design the how.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) True or false: a PM's authority mainly comes from managing engineers as their boss. 2) Name the three concerns a PM must keep in balance. 3) A stakeholder demands a specific feature 'by Friday.' What is the first question a good PM asks? 4) Who typically owns the detailed technical design of a solution? 5) Give one behavior that builds a PM's influence. Answers: 1) False - most PMs have no direct reports; influence comes from clarity and trust. 2) Customer needs, business goals, and technical feasibility. 3) 'What problem are we trying to solve, and for whom?' 4) Engineering (with the PM setting the requirements, not the implementation). 5) Knowing the customer and data deeply, and writing clearly.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing being 'the CEO of the product' with being the boss of the team - the PM leads through influence, not command. Mistake: jumping to solutions and skipping the problem. Exit: (a) Does a PM normally manage the engineers as their direct reports? (b) What does the PM own that the team does not? Answers: no; the problem and the priorities (the why and the what).

lessons.title: Discovering customer problems: interviews and jobs-to-be-done
lessons.grammar_note: In an interview, ask about past behavior ('tell me about the last time...') rather than future intentions ('would you use...') - people predict their own behavior poorly but report the past more reliably.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Run a problem-discovery interview, avoid leading questions, and frame a need as a job to be done rather than a feature request. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, does jobs-to-be-done focus on the feature a customer names or the progress they want to make?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Before building anything, a PM has to learn what problem is worth solving and for whom. The most reliable way is talking to real customers. Good discovery interviews dig into concrete past experiences, not hypothetical futures: you ask people to walk through the last time they faced the situation, what they were trying to accomplish, and what got in the way. The jobs-to-be-done lens reframes this: customers do not want a quarter-inch drill, they want a quarter-inch hole - and really, a shelf on the wall. When you understand the underlying job, the progress the person is trying to make, you can serve it in ways they never would have requested by name. This protects you from building exactly what a customer asked for and still missing the point.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Leading question (weak): 'Wouldn't you love a faster export button?' It invites a yes and teaches you nothing. Open question (strong): 'Tell me about the last time you needed to get data out of the tool - what were you doing, and what happened?' Feature framing: 'Users want a dark mode.' Job framing: 'When I work late, I want to reduce eye strain so that I can keep going comfortably' - which dark mode might serve, but so might adjustable brightness. Another: a bank found customers requesting 'more branches,' but the underlying job was 'deposit a check without leaving home,' better served by a phone camera than by new buildings.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Rewrite the leading question 'Do you think our new dashboard is great?' as an open, behavior-based question. 2) In the drill example, what is the deeper job? 3) Which is more reliable: asking what someone did last week, or what they might do next month? 4) Turn 'the user wants a bulk-upload feature' into a job-to-be-done statement. 5) Name one sign you are asking a leading question. Answers: 1) Something like 'Walk me through the last time you used the dashboard - what were you trying to find?' 2) Putting up a shelf (making progress in their space), not owning a drill. 3) What they did last week - past behavior is a better guide than predicted behavior. 4) e.g. 'When I onboard a new client, I want to add all their records at once so that I can start work the same day.' 5) It can be answered yes or no, or it hints at the answer you want.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: asking customers to design the solution for you ('what feature do you want?') instead of describing their problem. Mistake: trusting stated future intentions over observed past behavior. Exit: (a) Should discovery questions target past behavior or future hypotheticals? (b) What does a job-to-be-done describe? Answers: past behavior; the progress or outcome a customer is trying to achieve, independent of any specific feature.

lessons.title: Prioritization: RICE, MoSCoW, and value vs effort
lessons.grammar_note: Prioritization frameworks are tools for a conversation, not a calculator that decides for you - the numbers organize judgment; they do not replace it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Score ideas with RICE, sort requirements with MoSCoW, and place work on a value-versus-effort grid to decide what to do next. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which RICE factor sits in the denominator?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: There are always more things to build than time to build them, so a PM needs a defensible way to choose. RICE scores each idea as (Reach x Impact x Confidence) / Effort: Reach is how many users are affected in a period, Impact is how much it moves the goal per user, Confidence is how sure you are of your estimates (often a percentage), and Effort is the work required. A higher score means a better bet. MoSCoW instead sorts requirements into Must have, Should have, Could have, and Won't have (this time), which is quick and great for scoping a release. The value-versus-effort grid plots each item by expected value and cost; the 'high value, low effort' quadrant holds the quick wins you tackle first, while 'low value, high effort' items are the money pits to avoid.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: RICE: Feature A reaches 2,000 users, impact 2 (massive), confidence 80% (0.8), effort 4 person-weeks: score = (2000 x 2 x 0.8) / 4 = 800. Feature B reaches 500, impact 1, confidence 100% (1.0), effort 1: score = (500 x 1 x 1.0) / 1 = 500. A wins. MoSCoW for a first release of a checkout: Must have - accept payment; Should have - save card for later; Could have - gift wrapping; Won't have (yet) - loyalty points. Value vs effort: a one-line copy fix that lifts conversion is high value, low effort - a quick win; a full billing-system rewrite is high effort and, if it does not change customer outcomes soon, low near-term value.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Compute the RICE score for Reach 1,000, Impact 3, Confidence 0.5, Effort 3. 2) In MoSCoW, which bucket means 'not in this release'? 3) On the value/effort grid, which quadrant do you schedule first? 4) Feature X scores RICE 300, Feature Y scores 900 - which comes first, all else equal? 5) Why keep Confidence in RICE at all? Answers: 1) (1000 x 3 x 0.5) / 3 = 500. 2) Won't have (this time). 3) High value, low effort - the quick wins. 4) Feature Y (higher score). 5) It discounts ideas built on shaky estimates, so a shiny but unproven bet does not automatically win.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating the RICE number as a verdict instead of a prompt to discuss assumptions. Mistake: letting 'Should have' quietly become 'Must have' until every item is a must and nothing is prioritized. Exit: (a) Write the RICE formula. (b) Which value/effort quadrant should you generally avoid? Answers: (Reach x Impact x Confidence) / Effort; high effort, low value.

questions.prompt: A PM's influence over a team without direct reports comes mainly from...
questions.explanation: PMs lead through influence - deep understanding and clear communication - not authority.

questions.prompt: Which interview question is least likely to mislead you?
options: Wouldn't you love a faster app?
Would you pay for this someday?
Tell me about the last time you tried to do this task.
Isn't our design the best you've seen?
questions.explanation: Asking about concrete past behavior yields more reliable signal than leading or hypothetical questions.

questions.prompt: Compute the RICE score for Reach 2,000, Impact 2, Confidence 0.8, Effort 4.
In MoSCoW, an item you will deliberately exclude from the current release is labeled...
questions.explanation: Won't have (this time) names what is intentionally out of scope now.

questions.prompt: A quarter-inch drill customer 'really' wants...
options: a quarter-inch hole (and the shelf it enables)
questions.explanation: Jobs-to-be-done: the customer wants the outcome, not the tool for its own sake.

questions.prompt: On a value-versus-effort grid, 'quick wins' are...
questions.explanation: High value for low effort is the quadrant you schedule first.

lessons.title: Writing a PRD and user stories
lessons.grammar_note: A user story is a promise to have a conversation, not a full spec - the detail lives in the acceptance criteria and in talking with the team, not in ever-longer sentences.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Write a product requirements document (PRD) that states the problem, goals, and scope, and break work into user stories with clear acceptance criteria. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what does the 'so that' clause of a user story capture?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A PRD is the document that gets everyone on the same page before building. A useful PRD is short and answers: what problem are we solving and for whom, why now, what does success look like (the metric), what is in scope and explicitly out of scope, and what are the key requirements and constraints. It states the what and why, and leaves most of the how to design and engineering. User stories translate the PRD into small, buildable pieces, each written as 'As a [user], I want [capability], so that [benefit].' Each story carries acceptance criteria - concrete, testable conditions that define 'done,' often written as 'Given / When / Then.' Good stories are small enough to finish quickly and independent enough to ship on their own.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A tight PRD problem statement: 'New users abandon onboarding at the email-verification step (42% drop-off). Goal: raise activation from 55% to 65% this quarter. Out of scope: redesigning the whole signup flow.' A user story: 'As a new user, I want to resend the verification email, so that I can finish signing up if the first message never arrives.' Acceptance criteria: 'Given I am on the verification screen, When I click Resend, Then a new email is sent within 30 seconds and I see a confirmation message; the button is disabled for 60 seconds to prevent spamming.' Notice the criteria are testable - a reviewer can check each one.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Fill in the template: 'As a ___, I want ___, so that ___,' for a user who wants to export a report to PDF. 2) Name two things a PRD should put explicitly out of scope for a first release. 3) Rewrite this vague criterion as testable: 'The page should be fast.' 4) What format is commonly used for acceptance criteria? 5) True or false: a PRD should specify the exact database tables to use. Answers: 1) e.g. 'As an analyst, I want to export a report to PDF, so that I can share it with a client who has no account.' 2) e.g. multi-language support and custom themes - anything not needed to solve the core problem now. 3) e.g. 'Given a typical report, When I open the page, Then it becomes interactive within 2 seconds.' 4) Given / When / Then. 5) False - that is engineering's decision; the PRD states requirements, not implementation.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: writing a giant PRD that specifies the solution in detail and boxes in the engineers. Mistake: acceptance criteria that cannot actually be tested ('should feel intuitive'). Exit: (a) Give the three-part user-story template. (b) What makes an acceptance criterion good? Answers: 'As a [user], I want [capability], so that [benefit]'; it is concrete and testable, so anyone can verify whether it is met.

lessons.title: Working with design and engineering: agile basics
lessons.grammar_note: 'Agile' is a set of values - ship small, get feedback, adapt - not a rigid ceremony. Scrum and Kanban are two ways to practice it, not the point of it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how a cross-functional team collaborates day to day, explain the basics of agile, Scrum, and Kanban, and name the PM's role in each ritual. Warm-up: who owns the detailed technical design of a solution - the PM or engineering?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Modern products are built by small cross-functional teams - a PM, designers, and engineers - working closely rather than handing documents over a wall. Agile is the umbrella philosophy: build in small increments, put working software in front of users, gather feedback, and adapt, instead of planning everything up front. Scrum is one popular framework: work happens in short fixed cycles called sprints (often two weeks), with a few rituals - sprint planning (decide what to tackle), a daily standup (quick sync on progress and blockers), a review (show what shipped), and a retrospective (improve how the team works). Kanban is a lighter alternative: a continuous flow of work pulled from a prioritized backlog, visualized on a board, with limits on how much is in progress at once. The PM's steady contributions are a well-ordered backlog and clear priorities; the PM does not assign tasks or estimate the engineering work.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Scrum in motion: at planning, the team pulls the top stories from the backlog into a two-week sprint; each morning's standup surfaces that the payment integration is blocked on a missing credential; the review demos the finished resend-email flow; the retrospective agrees to add credentials to the setup checklist. Kanban in motion: a support team keeps a board with columns To Do, In Progress, and Done, caps In Progress at three items so nothing stalls half-finished, and simply pulls the next-highest priority whenever a slot frees up. In both, the PM keeps the backlog ordered so the team always pulls the most valuable work next; the engineers decide how long each item takes.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the short, fixed work cycle in Scrum called? 2) Name the four common Scrum rituals. 3) In Kanban, what does a work-in-progress limit prevent? 4) Whose job is it to estimate how long a story will take - the PM or the engineers? 5) Give the one-sentence spirit of agile. Answers: 1) A sprint. 2) Sprint planning, daily standup, review, and retrospective. 3) Too many things started and none finished - it keeps work flowing to done. 4) The engineers who will build it. 5) Build small, get real feedback, and adapt - rather than planning everything up front.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating agile rituals as box-ticking while ignoring the goal of fast feedback. Mistake: the PM dictating task estimates or micromanaging how engineers work. Exit: (a) Name Scrum's short work cycle. (b) What is the PM's main ongoing input to the team, whatever the framework? Answers: the sprint; a clearly prioritized backlog.

lessons.title: Roadmapping and stakeholder alignment
lessons.grammar_note: A roadmap communicates intent and priority over time; it is a plan, not a promise. State confidence honestly: near-term items are firm, far-term items are directional.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Build a roadmap organized around outcomes, keep it honest about certainty, and align stakeholders who want different things. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what should a good roadmap communicate instead of exact dates a year out?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A roadmap is how a PM communicates where the product is heading and why, over time. The strongest roadmaps are organized around outcomes and priorities - the problems you intend to solve and the order - rather than a precise calendar of features. A common structure is Now / Next / Later: Now is committed and fairly certain, Next is likely but still shaping, and Later is directional and subject to change. This lets you commit near-term without over-promising the distant future. Stakeholders - executives, sales, support, marketing - each push for their own priorities, so alignment is a core PM skill: you surface the shared goal, make trade-offs explicit ('yes to this means not that, this quarter'), and tie decisions back to customer and business value. Alignment is not pleasing everyone; it is a shared, transparent understanding of why the priorities are what they are.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A Now/Next/Later roadmap for a support tool: Now - cut first-response time (shipping canned replies and routing); Next - reduce repeat tickets (self-serve help center); Later - explore proactive outreach. Notice each entry names an outcome, not just a feature. Alignment in action: sales wants a big enterprise feature, support wants bug fixes, and the data shows churn is driven by reliability. The PM frames the trade-off openly: 'We can do the enterprise feature or the reliability work this quarter, not both; churn is our biggest risk, so reliability is Now and the enterprise feature is Next.' The decision is documented with its reasoning, so even those who disagree understand why.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In a Now/Next/Later roadmap, which column is most certain? 2) Should a roadmap item read 'Ship feature X on March 3' or 'Reduce first-response time'? 3) A PM says yes to everyone and commits to it all. What has gone wrong? 4) Name two stakeholder groups a PM commonly aligns. 5) What is alignment really about - agreement or shared understanding? Answers: 1) Now - it is committed and near-term. 2) The outcome, 'Reduce first-response time'; the feature is one way to get there. 3) Over-committing - without trade-offs, priorities become meaningless and dates slip. 4) e.g. sales and support (also executives, marketing, engineering). 5) Shared, transparent understanding of the why - not everyone agreeing.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: publishing a date-stamped feature list far into the future and treating it as a contract. Mistake: seeking alignment by quietly promising each group what it wants. Exit: (a) What should roadmap entries emphasize - outcomes or exact dates? (b) In Now/Next/Later, which bucket is directional and most likely to change? Answers: outcomes (and priority); Later.

questions.prompt: The 'so that' clause in a user story states the...
options: benefit or reason the user wants it
questions.explanation: It ties the story to the value the user is after.

questions.prompt: A good acceptance criterion is one that is...
questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria must be checkable so 'done' is unambiguous, often in Given/When/Then form.

questions.prompt: In Scrum, the short fixed cycle of work is called a...
questions.explanation: Work happens in sprints, often two weeks long.

questions.prompt: A Kanban work-in-progress limit exists to...
options: prevent too many unfinished items piling up
questions.explanation: WIP limits keep work flowing to done instead of everything being half-started.

questions.prompt: In a Now / Next / Later roadmap, the most certain, committed work sits under...
questions.explanation: Now is near-term and committed; Later is directional and likely to change.

questions.prompt: Stakeholder alignment is best understood as...
options: a shared, transparent understanding of the priorities and why
questions.explanation: Alignment means everyone understands the reasoning, even when they would have chosen differently.

lessons.title: Defining and tracking metrics: North Star and funnels
lessons.grammar_note: Beware vanity metrics - numbers that only go up and flatter you (total signups ever) without reflecting real value. Prefer metrics tied to customer outcomes and to a specific time window.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Choose a North Star metric, break a user journey into a funnel, and read conversion rates to find where users drop off. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what is a North Star metric meant to capture?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: You cannot improve what you do not measure, so a PM defines the numbers that reflect real progress. A North Star metric is the single measure that best captures the core value customers get from the product - for a messaging app it might be messages sent between real contacts, for a marketplace it might be completed transactions. It aligns the whole team on delivered value rather than activity. Beneath it, a funnel breaks a journey into ordered steps - for example visit, sign up, activate, pay, retain - and you track the conversion rate from each step to the next. Where a big percentage of users fall out is where the biggest opportunity usually lives. Good metrics avoid the vanity trap: cumulative totals that only rise look nice but hide whether you are actually creating value now; rates, active-user counts, and retention over a defined period tell you far more.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: North Star choices: for a video platform, 'watch-time from satisfied viewers'; for a to-do app, 'weekly tasks completed.' Each points at value, not vanity. Funnel math: of 1,000 visitors, 200 sign up (20% visit-to-signup), 100 activate (50% signup-to-activate), 30 pay (30% activate-to-pay). The steepest drop is visit-to-signup at 80% lost, so that step is the first place to investigate. Vanity vs useful: 'we have 1 million total signups since launch' is vanity - it never goes down and hides churn; 'we have 40,000 weekly active users, up from 35,000' reflects present value. Pairing a rate with a time window ('30-day retention is 42%') keeps you honest.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A funnel has 500 signups and 150 activations. What is the signup-to-activation conversion rate? 2) Which is a vanity metric: total downloads ever, or 7-day retention? 3) For a ride-hailing app, propose a North Star metric. 4) In the worked funnel, which step had the largest drop-off? 5) Why attach a time window to a metric like retention? Answers: 1) 150 / 500 = 30%. 2) Total downloads ever - it only grows and hides churn. 3) e.g. completed rides per week (a value-reflecting measure). 4) Visit-to-signup (80% of visitors did not sign up). 5) Without a window 'retention' is ambiguous; '30-day retention' states exactly what and over how long you are measuring.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: celebrating a cumulative total that can never fall and treating it as progress. Mistake: tracking dozens of metrics with no single North Star, so the team optimizes in different directions. Exit: (a) What does a North Star metric represent? (b) In a funnel, what does a conversion rate measure? Answers: the core value customers get from the product; the fraction of users who move from one step to the next.

lessons.title: Experimentation and A/B testing
lessons.grammar_note: Change one thing at a time and decide your success metric and sample size before you start - peeking early and stopping the moment a result looks good is how teams fool themselves.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Design a simple A/B test, define a hypothesis and a success metric, and avoid the common ways experiments mislead. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what role does the control group play?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Rather than argue about opinions, PMs often let experimentation settle the question. An A/B test splits users randomly into two groups: the control keeps the current experience while the variant gets one change. Because assignment is random, differences in the outcome can be attributed to that change. You start with a hypothesis - 'making the signup button larger and greener will increase signup completion' - and a single success metric decided in advance. You then run the test until you have gathered enough data (a sample size chosen up front) for the result to be trustworthy, and only then read the outcome. The discipline matters: change one variable so you know what caused any difference, do not stop the moment the numbers look favorable, and remember that a difference must be large and stable enough to be real, not random noise.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A clean test: hypothesis 'a shorter signup form raises completion'; control shows the current 8-field form, variant shows a 4-field form; success metric is signup-completion rate; you decide in advance to run until 10,000 users have seen each version. Result: control converts at 20%, variant at 26% over the full sample - a real, sizable lift, so you ship the shorter form. A flawed test: the team changes the form length and the button color and the headline all at once, so when conversion moves, nobody can say which change did it. Another trap: after two hours the variant is 'winning' by a hair on 40 users, the team ships it, and the effect vanishes at scale because it was noise.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In an A/B test, which group keeps the existing experience? 2) Why change only one variable at a time? 3) A test looks positive after 30 users. Should you stop and ship? 4) Write a one-line hypothesis for testing a new empty-state screen. 5) Why decide the success metric before running the test? Answers: 1) The control group. 2) So any difference in the outcome can be attributed to that single change, not to a mix of changes. 3) No - 30 users is far too few; wait for the planned sample so the result is not just noise. 4) e.g. 'Adding a guided empty-state screen will increase the share of new users who create their first project.' 5) So you cannot rationalize a favorable-looking number after the fact; the goal is fixed before you see the data.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: testing several changes at once and losing the ability to attribute the result. Mistake: stopping the test the instant it looks good ('peeking') on a tiny sample. Exit: (a) What is the control group? (b) Name one discipline that keeps an experiment honest. Answers: the group that keeps the current, unchanged experience as a baseline; changing one variable at a time, or fixing the metric and sample size before starting.

lessons.title: Go-to-market and launch
lessons.grammar_note: 'Launch' is not the finish line; it is the start of learning. Plan how you will measure adoption and gather feedback after release, not just the announcement itself.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Put together a basic go-to-market plan, choose an appropriate launch approach, and define what a successful launch looks like. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what question does go-to-market planning primarily answer?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Building something is only half the job; a go-to-market (GTM) plan is how the right customers discover it, understand its value, and adopt it. A GTM plan names the target customer, the core message (the value proposition in plain language), the channels to reach them (email, sales, in-product, content, partners), and the success criteria for the launch. Launches also come in sizes: a quiet internal or 'dogfood' release to your own team, a limited beta to a small set of friendly users, a phased or percentage rollout that exposes the change to a growing slice of users, and a full public launch. Smaller first steps let you catch problems before everyone sees them. Coordination is a big part of the PM's launch role: making sure support has documentation, sales and marketing know the message, and engineering is ready to monitor and roll back if something breaks.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A staged launch: week 1, dogfood to the internal team to shake out obvious bugs; week 2, beta to 50 friendly customers who opted in; week 3, roll out to 10% of users while watching error rates and the activation metric; week 4, go to 100% once the numbers hold. A GTM one-pager: target - small e-commerce teams; message - 'recover abandoned carts without writing code'; channels - onboarding email, in-app announcement, a help-center article; success - 15% of eligible accounts enable the feature in the first month. Notice the PM lines up support docs and a monitoring plan before the wide release, so a spike in errors triggers a rollback rather than a fire drill.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the four elements of a basic GTM plan. 2) Order these from smallest to largest audience: public launch, beta, dogfood, phased rollout. 3) Why launch to 10% of users before 100%? 4) Give a plausible success criterion for launching a referral feature. 5) True or false: the PM's job ends when the feature is announced. Answers: 1) Target customer, core message/value proposition, channels, and success criteria. 2) Dogfood, beta, phased rollout, public launch. 3) To catch problems on a small audience and roll back cheaply before everyone is affected. 4) e.g. '10% of active users send at least one referral in the first month.' 5) False - launch begins the learning; you then measure adoption and iterate.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating the announcement as the goal and ignoring whether customers actually adopt and succeed. Mistake: a big-bang launch to everyone with no staging, no monitoring, and no rollback plan. Exit: (a) What does a GTM plan help the right customers do? (b) Why prefer a phased rollout over an instant full launch? Answers: discover the product, understand its value, and adopt it; it limits the blast radius of problems and lets you learn and roll back before full exposure.

questions.prompt: A North Star metric should reflect...
options: how many meetings the team holds
the core value customers get from the product
the number of lines of code written
questions.explanation: It captures delivered customer value and aligns the team around it.

questions.prompt: Of 1,000 visitors, 200 sign up. The visit-to-signup conversion rate is...
Which is a vanity metric?
questions.explanation: A cumulative total only rises and hides churn, flattering you without showing present value.

questions.prompt: In an A/B test, changing only one variable at a time lets you...
options: attribute any difference in outcome to that specific change
questions.explanation: Isolating one change is what makes the result interpretable.

questions.prompt: Which launch approach exposes a change to a growing slice of users over time?
questions.explanation: A phased rollout grows the audience gradually so problems stay contained.

questions.prompt: A basic go-to-market plan should define the target customer, the core message, the channels, and...
options: the success criteria for the launch
questions.explanation: Success criteria tell you whether the launch actually worked.

lessons.title: Capstone: spec a feature end to end
lessons.grammar_note: A strong spec connects a real problem to a measurable outcome: problem, then solution, then how you will know it worked. If you cannot state the metric, the spec is not finished.

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Pick a product you use and choose one real problem its users face. Write a short feature spec that carries the problem all the way to a launch and a metric, using everything from this course. Aim for one to two pages: crisp, honest, and testable - the kind of document you could hand to a design-and-engineering team to start work.

sections.heading: The structure to follow
sections.text: 1) Problem and audience: state the problem and who has it, ideally grounded in a job-to-be-done ('when I..., I want..., so that...'). 2) Evidence: one or two signals that this is real (an interview quote, a funnel drop-off, a support trend). 3) Goal metric: the single number success will move, with a target and a time window. 4) Proposed solution: the core idea at a high level plus two or three user stories with acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then form; state what is explicitly out of scope. 5) Prioritization: a RICE score or a value/effort placement showing why this is worth doing now. 6) Launch and measurement: the rollout approach (dogfood, beta, phased, full) and how you will read the goal metric, including whether an A/B test is warranted.

sections.heading: A worked mini-example
sections.text: Problem: 'When a new user finishes signup, they land on an empty dashboard and do not know what to do, so many never create their first project.' Evidence: activation (first project created) sits at 45%, and five interviews mention confusion at the empty screen. Goal metric: raise 7-day activation from 45% to 55% this quarter. Solution: a guided empty state with a one-click 'create sample project.' Story: 'As a new user, I want a guided first step, so that I can see value quickly.' Acceptance: 'Given an empty dashboard, When I click Create sample project, Then a prefilled project opens within 3 seconds and a checklist of next steps appears.' Out of scope: a full onboarding tour. Prioritization: RICE - Reach 3,000 new users/month, Impact 2, Confidence 0.7, Effort 3 = (3000 x 2 x 0.7)/3 = 1,400, high versus alternatives. Launch: dogfood, then beta to 100 new users, then an A/B test at 50/50 measuring 7-day activation before full rollout.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer these to pressure-test your own spec before you consider it done. 1) Is your problem framed as a job-to-be-done or as a pre-chosen feature? 2) Can your goal metric actually be measured, and does it have a time window? 3) Are your acceptance criteria testable by someone else? 4) Does your prioritization show why now, not just that the idea is nice? 5) Does your plan say how you will learn after launch? Answers: 1) It should be a job-to-be-done - if it names a feature first, restate the underlying problem. 2) Yes - if you cannot measure it or it lacks a window (e.g. '7-day activation'), tighten it. 3) Yes - rewrite any 'should feel nice' criterion into Given/When/Then. 4) It should reference a RICE score or value/effort position, not just enthusiasm. 5) Yes - name the rollout stages and whether an A/B test applies; a launch with no measurement plan is unfinished.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: Check yes to each: the problem is stated as a job-to-be-done for a specific audience; there is at least one piece of real evidence; there is exactly one goal metric with a target and a time window; the solution includes user stories with testable Given/When/Then acceptance criteria and an explicit out-of-scope line; prioritization is justified with RICE or value/effort; and the launch section names a rollout approach and how the metric will be read. If all six are true, you have written a spec that connects a real problem to a measurable outcome - the heart of the product manager's craft.

questions.prompt: The clearest description of a product manager's core responsibility is...
options: writing and shipping the code themselves
deciding what to build and why, then aligning a team to ship it
questions.explanation: The PM owns the problem and priorities and leads the team to a solution - Lesson 2.

questions.prompt: The most reliable discovery-interview question asks about...
options: what the user might do next year
whether the user likes your idea
a concrete past experience the user actually had
which feature the user would design
questions.explanation: Past behavior is a better guide than hypotheticals or leading questions - Lesson 3.

questions.prompt: Jobs-to-be-done reframes 'the user wants a dark mode' as...
options: the user wants any new color
when working late, I want to reduce eye strain so I can keep going
the user wants a brighter screen
questions.explanation: It surfaces the underlying progress, which several solutions could serve - Lesson 3.

questions.prompt: Compute the RICE score for Reach 1,000, Impact 3, Confidence 0.5, Effort 3.
A well-formed user story follows the shape...
options: As a [user], I want [capability], so that [benefit]
questions.explanation: The three-part template keeps the story tied to a user and a benefit - Lesson 6.

questions.prompt: A good acceptance criterion is written to be...
options: concrete and testable, often as Given/When/Then
questions.explanation: Testable criteria make 'done' unambiguous - Lesson 6.

questions.prompt: In Scrum, the recurring fixed-length work cycle is the...
questions.explanation: Teams commit to a set of work each sprint, often two weeks - Lesson 7.

questions.prompt: In a Now / Next / Later roadmap, the 'Later' column is...
options: directional and most likely to change
questions.explanation: Later expresses intent, not a promise, and is expected to shift - Lesson 8.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a vanity metric?
questions.explanation: A cumulative total only rises and hides churn - Lesson 10.

questions.prompt: A funnel of 1,000 visitors -> 200 signups -> 100 activations has an overall visit-to-activation rate of...
questions.explanation: 100 activations / 1,000 visitors = 10% - Lesson 10.

questions.prompt: The control group in an A/B test exists to...
options: receive every new change at once
serve as an unchanged baseline for comparison
shorten the test to a few users
replace the need for a success metric
questions.explanation: Comparing the variant against an unchanged control isolates the effect of the change - Lesson 11.

questions.prompt: The safest way to release a risky change to a large user base is...
options: a full big-bang launch with no monitoring
a phased or percentage rollout with monitoring and a rollback plan
questions.explanation: A staged rollout limits the blast radius and lets you roll back - Lesson 12.

questions.prompt: A go-to-market plan must define the target customer, the core message, the channels, and...
questions.explanation: Success criteria tell you whether the launch worked - Lesson 12.

questions.prompt: The unifying idea of a strong feature spec is that it...
options: lists as many features as possible
connects a real problem to a measurable outcome
specifies the exact code to write
questions.explanation: Problem -> solution -> how you will know it worked is the heart of the craft - Lesson 14.
